newsitem.title: USA: Thai economy faces test post-baht fall-US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy faces test post-baht fall-US analysts.

text.p: Structural problems that strained Thailand's economic growth and invited speculative attacks on its currency will not see a quick fix from the floating exchange rate regime, U.S. economists said.
In fact, they argued that the "hard landing" of the Thai economy has yet to hit bottom, as the floating baht brings relief to some sectors and increases hardship on others.
"People tend to think devaluation is a discrete event," said Thomas Trebat, head of emerging markets research at Citicorp Securities.
"The regimen in the aftermath is more important than the devaluation itself," Trebat said.
Thailand's government on July 2 abandoned pegging the baht's value on a basket of major currencies and effectively devalued the currency by some 15 percent.

The baht's float took place five weeks after the Czech Republic gave up its semi-fixed exchange rate and let the koruna drop. Investors are watching closely how each country pursues austerity measures and deals with the economic and social consequences, Trebat said.

However, Thailand, because of its size and long history of openness to foreign investment, is more appropriately compared with Mexico than with the Czech Republic, even though the scale of its financial crisis was much smaller, he noted.

Trebat explained that in a classic scenario, devaluation is followed by slowing growth, declining tax revenues, higher interest rates and increasing difficulties in debt servicing. Only later would credit ease, job-creation rise and consumer spending resume.

Exports are the engine driving the recovery. That is precisely where the Thai economy ran into a head wind because of its inability to move up the value chain, he said. "Thailand may become more competitive against its southeast Asian neighbors, but that is only on the margin."

Gregory Fager, head of the Asia division of the Institute of International Finance, agreed that a weaker currency could help revive Thailand's flagging export sector of low-valued goods, such as in textiles. However, in other areas, a lack of skilled labor would still hamper export growth, he added.
"The structural problem in the economy is far more important than can be addressed by the exchange rate," he said, adding: "We see underlying weakness of the economy as very severe."

Another structural weakness urgently in need of reform is the troubled finance sector. That clean-up operation could strain available resources, market sources said. "The task is to find the level to write down the bad loans and to resume turnover in the real estate area," said an analyst at an investment bank, noting it took years for the U.S. government to sort out the savings and loan fiasco of the 1980s.
Geoffrey Dennis, head of emerging market research at HSBC James Capel, said investors should be patient as the Thai government tries to stabilize the financial sector. "The repair work takes time."
In the process, banks and finance companies without cashflow difficulties would emerge stronger, he said. "We see a shakedown rather than a shakeout."
The Thai government has taken steps to force 16 insolvent financial companies to merge with healthy ones.
"They have finally come to grips with coralling the problem, but there is a long way between that and solving the problem," said Fager of the Institute of International Finance.
